See [the reusable kernel contract](kernel.md) for application ownership and the
non-research execution proof, and [installation boundaries](installations.md) for
independent records and runtime lifecycles. These remain inside this repository.

The local [improvement application](improvements.md) uses that same kernel contract
in an explicitly new experiment record. Captured public research informs code
proposals; it does not become writable research authority. Untrusted candidate
code runs only in restricted disposable containers, while the host scores its
outputs. An operator review receipt cannot apply code or grant release authority.

The [autonomous context lane](autonomous-context.md) is a separate WAKE application
policy on the existing per-node native authority. An installed capability permits
one selector-field change, gated by recomputed fixed-task and current-native-state
measurements. Proposal generation, adoption and rollback require no per-change
human review. Metadata events preserve research versions and history; candidate
data cannot replace the evaluator, widen permissions, modify code or create a
competing research store. Native replay owns the policy after restart.

> **Current specification.** This document explains why the present system is shaped this way: its trust boundary, durable record, governance model and known limits. Current local procedures belong in `standalone.md`; public mirror publishing belongs in `cloud.md`. Maintainer navigation, environment checks and reproducible validation guidance belong in `development.md`.

**WAKE✳︎** is infrastructure for continuity of accountable work, not continuity of a model instance. Its stable sequence is **Record → Context → Proposal → Governance → Transition → Receipt**. {"url": "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all%3Aepistemic+peer+disagreement+criteria+for+preferring+independent+evidence+over+consensus&max_results=4", "scope": "paper abstracts; preprints, peer-review status not verified", "excerpt": "title: Peer-to-Peer Secure Multi-Party Numerical Computation
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/0810.1624v1
published: 2008-10-09T13:07:36Z
summary: We propose an efficient framework for enabling secure multi-party numerical computations in a Peer-to-Peer network. This problem arises in a range of applications such as collaborative filtering, distributed computation of trust and reputation, monitoring and numerous other tasks, where the computing nodes would like to preserve the privacy of their inputs while performing a joint computation of a certain function.
  Although there is a rich literature in the field of distributed systems security concerning secure multi-party computation, in practice it is hard to deploy those methods in very large scale Peer-to-Peer networks. In this work, we examine several possible approaches and discuss their feasibility. Among the possible approaches, we identify a single approach which is both scalable and theoretically secure.
  An additional novel contribution is that we show how to compute the neighborhood based collaborative filtering, a state-of-the-art collaborative filtering algorithm, winner of the Netflix progress prize of the year 2007. Our solution computes this algorithm in a Peer-to-Peer network, using a privacy preserving computation, without loss of accuracy.
  Using extensive large scale simulations on top of real Internet topologies, we demonstrate the applicability of our approach. As far as we know, we are the first to implement such a large scale secure multi-party simulation of networks of millions of nodes and hundreds of millions of edges.

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=cognitive+architecture+models+distinguishing+between+transient+behavioral+states+and+stable+preference+traits&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Dynamic Digital Detachment and Work-Family Permeability: The Interactive Regulatory Path of Personality and Cognitive Load.\", \"abstract\": \"

Introduction

Mobile connectivity has worn the work-home boundary thin for employees born after 1995, prompting some to deliberately disconnect from work-related digital channels during nonwork time. Whether this digital detachment reliably narrows work-family permeability, and for whom, has been obscured by static cross-sectional designs that treat permeability as fixed rather than as a process unfolding across days.

Methods

Using a two-week experience-sampling study of 192 digitally native Chinese employees aged 22-29 (53.6% women), yielding 2304 day-level observations, we modeled the trajectory of permeability with multilevel growth and cross-lagged panel specifications.

Results

On days when employees disconnected more than their own average, permeability was lower both the same evening (within-person coefficient about -0.31) and one day later (about -0.24), and this association appeared to strengthen over the sampling period rather than fade overnight. The pattern was conditional on a second-order interaction between stable traits and fluctuating cognitive load: among conscientious workers the association held even on heavy days, whereas among neurotic workers it weakened to non-significance once load ran high.

Discussion

Because the data are observational and longitudinal rather than experimental, we frame these findings as associations rather than causal effects. They nonetheless recast boundary work as a daily, effortful, and conditionally successful act, extend conservation of resources theory and boundary theory into the digital domain, and caution against uniform after-hours disconnection mandates in favor of support weighted toward overloaded and emotionally reactive workers.\", \"doi\": \"10.2147/prbm.s632561\", \"pmid\": \"42781609\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13600267\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscr…

7: ## Run one installation container
8: 
9: The current local path is one `wake` container, one web server, and twelve internal
10: worker processes called nodes. Three parents (`100.wake`, `200.wake`, `300.wake`)
11: each have three children. Nodes do not run their own web servers. The installation
12: controller starts, stops, and routes them; they cannot continue after it exits.
13: Each node retains its own governed SQLite record. The controller has no separate
14: writable group research database.
15: 
16: Prepare topics and provider settings, then build and launch from the repository:
17: 
18: ```sh
19: test -f .env || cp .env.example .env
20: test -f research-topics.toml || cp example.research-topics.toml research-topics.toml
21: # Configure GEMINI_API_KEY if you intend to enable Gemini later.
22: # Edit your local research-topics.toml for this installation.
23: ./scripts/wake_installation build
24: ./scripts/wake_installation start
25: ./scripts/wake_installation shell
26: wake-research --help
28: ```
29: 
30: **Every container launch starts research stopped.** Inspection does not enable
31: research or Bob calls. The Console and shell are available first;
32: use `wake-research start` only after inspecting the installation and configuration.
